title: TA9-07897
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXXXXX ("the principal claimant"), his wife, Jarmila XXXXX ("the female claimant"), XXXXXXXXX (the "daughter" claimant) and her two minor-age children, XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXX (the "minor" claimants) are all citizens of the Czech Republic and they seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the IRPA).

These claims were joined pursuant to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.2 The daughter claimant, XXXXXXXXX, was the designated representative for the minor children pursuant to section 167(2) of the IRPA. The Panel is of the opinion that the principal, female and daughter claimants must rely on each other's testimony to support their respective refugee claims.
The Panel notes that all of the claimants in this proceeding are relying on the PIF narrative3 of the principal claimant to support their respective claims.

The principal claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative4 describes a series of anti-Roma incidents, which were his and his associated family's catalyst to leave the Czech Republic and come to Canada to seek refugee status. Some of the incidents were briefly described and included the principal claimant's granddaughter being ostracized, verbally abused and assaulted by other children at her school in the Czech Republic for simply being an ethnic Romani. The female claimant was subjected to discriminatory treatment at a hairdressing salon, where she was refused service because she had no appointment but a non-Roma client was given service. The female claimant was also followed in stores when she was shopping, which she found demeaning.

In XXXXXX of 2008, the principal and female claimants were shopping in the town of XXXXX, where they were verbally and physically assaulted by four or five skinheads because of their Roma ethnicity. After this attack, these claimants went to the local police to report this incident and to make a complaint but they never heard back from the police with regard to this incident or the complaint. During a similar incident in XXXX of 2008, the daughter claimant and her boyfriend were verbally and physically attacked in a park by five or six skinheads because of their Roma ethnicity. They did make a police report but they heard nothing back with regard to this incident

The claimants are afraid of the German skinheads and the new neo-Nazi parties that hold rallies and marches near the Czech / German border, which is approximately two kilometres from where the claimants resided.
The claimants left the Czech Republic and arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009, where they filed claims as Convention refugees upon their arrival at the Toronto airport.

The Panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection. In arriving at this decision, the Panel has considered the issue of whether the claimants have provided credible and trustworthy evidence and the issue of whether the claimants' fear is objectively reasonable for these specific claimants as it pertains to the issues of discrimination versus persecution and the issue of a nexus to the definition of a Convention refugee. As well, the Panel has also considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in the Czech Republic, whether the principal claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. ANALYSIS Identity
The Panel determines that the claimants' supporting documentation, which includes their genuine Czech passports,5 establishes their identities as citizens of the Czech Republic. Credibility

Credibility is an issue in all claims before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). In order to determine whether the claim is well-founded, the Panel must find, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is credible and trustworthy. The Panel notes that a claimant's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness.6 The Panel believes that the existence of contradictions, discrepancies, and implausibilities in the evidence of a claimant is a well-accepted basis for a finding of a lack of credibility. This also applies to omissions in the principal claimant's previous statements, whether made to Canadian immigration officials at the time of arrival in Canada, in previous examinations under oath or at the hearing of the claim, or in his PIF. Credibility of the Claimant's Oral and Documentary Evidence

In oral submissions, counsel submitted that the evidence of the principal claimant was credible and that it supported his claim. The Panel does not agree. The Panel drew a number of negative credibility findings with regard to the principal claimant's PIF narrative and his oral testimony and the events that allegedly occurred in the Czech Republic.

In oral testimony, the principal claimant described the verbal and physical attack by skinheads in XXXXX, which allegedly occurred in XXXXXX of 2008, and his and the female claimant's attendance at the local police station to complain about this incident, where a police report was taken, however, he indicated that the police had never contacted him with regard to this report or any investigation. Although a police report was taken with regard to this alleged assault, the principal claimant indicted that he had not been given a copy of this report and he had never requested a copy of this document. In later testimony the principal claimant contradicted both his earlier oral testimony and his PIF narrative when he testified that he had been contacted and informed by the police that this matter was now closed because the "persons were unknown." The Panel noted the that the principal claimant's PIF narrative7 states, "We went to the police to make a complaint but we never heard back." The principal claimant confirmed this specific information in his PIF narrative was "true". After a series of questions, the principal claimant changed his testimony, he explained that they had actually been sent correspondence from the police a week after this incident had taken place and that the Czech police had closed this matter because the attackers were "unknown".

At this point in the hearing, the Panel noted and observed that the female claimant was attempting to prompt the principal claimant with regard to his testimony pertaining to the contradictions and inconsistencies between his oral testimony and his PIF narrative. The Panel made best efforts to request that the female claimant stop prompting the principal claimant.

The principal claimant was given another opportunity to explain this contradiction and he conceded that he had received police correspondence that the criminal matter was closed. As well, in response to the Panel's questions of why this document was not before it this day, the principal claimant indicated that he had left this specific correspondence in the Czech Republic. The principal claimant finally indicated that he was not aware that he would need these documents to support his refugee claim. The Panel gives this last explanation little weight since the instructions for question #31 of the PIF narrative are quite clear and they indicate, "On the following two pages, set out in chronological order all the significant events and reasons that have led you to claim refugee protection in Canada. ... Attach copies of any medical, psychological, police or other documents to support your claim." [emphasis within the document]. The principal and other claimants had a previous solicitor, who appears before the IRB on a regular basis and the Panel believes he would be familiar with the instructions for preparing a PIF narrative and the practice of corroborating statements with supporting documents, therefore, it is not reasonable or credible to the Panel that the principal claimant's previous solicitor would not have advised him to obtain any police documents pertaining to this alleged incident in the Czech Republic.

In Maldonado,8 the Federal Court stated, "[i]t has long been held that sworn testimony is to be believed, without corroboration, unless there is good reason not to believe it." According to paragraphs 203 and 204 of the UNHCR Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Establishing Refugee Status: After the applicant has made a genuine effort to substantiate his story there may still be a lack of evidence for some of his statements. ... it is hardly possible for a refugee to "prove" every part of his case and, indeed, if this were a requirement the majority of refugees would not be recognized. It is therefore frequently necessary to give the applicant the benefit of the doubt. The benefit of the doubt should, however, only be given when all available evidence has been obtained and checked and when the examiner is satisfied as to the applicant's general credibility.9

The Panel cannot extend the benefit of the doubt to the principal claimant with regard to his contradictory and inconsistent testimony, which goes directly to the issues of his reliability as a witness and the issues of a lack of state protection by the Czech police. The principal claimant admitted that he made no effort to get this alleged Czech police report, Czech police correspondence or any Czech medical reports with regard to his and his wife's attendance at a the police offices and medical clinic after this alleged attack. The Panel gives little weight to counsel's argument that the claimant would have difficulty getting this police report since the documentary evidence10 that counsel has quoted actually indicates "...according to Criminal Procedures Act No. 141/1961, an "injured party" (or his or her authorized agent or legal representative) has the right to inspect and make copies of all documents in the files of a legal proceeding, except for protected information, such as personal information about witnesses." In fact, the country-conditions documentation counsel has mentioned actually outlines the procedure for obtaining these corroborating documents even if the "injured party" is not in the Czech Republic. For all of these reasons, the Panel determines that the principal and female claimants have not made any concerted efforts to provide documentary evidence from the Czech Republic, which the Panel determines is reasonably available and could have supported these claims. For these reasons, the Panel draws a negative credibility finding with regard to the principal claimant's oral and documentary evidence.

The Panel notes that, during the commencement of the hearing, the principal claimant, female and daughter claimants confirmed that the information had been translated to them before they signed their respective declarations. In fact, the Panel notes that the Czech interpreter, XXXX XXXXX, had indicated with her signature that, "The claimant has indicated that he/she fully understands the entire content of this form and all attached documents and the answers provided, as interpreted by me."11 In addition, the principal claimant indicated with his own signature and date on the same page of his PIF that the information had been interpreted to him and that it was "complete, true and correct." The Panel gives little weight to the daughter claimant's explanation for the principal claimant's contradictory testimony, which was that he was nervous and may have been confused by the questions, since the Panel gave the principal several opportunities to explain these discrepancies and the Panel asked simple questions, which the principal claimant appeared to understand. Finally, in assessing this oral testimony, his PIF narrative and his explanations for this contradictory and inconsistent testimony, the Panel determines that the principal claimant has not explained this contradiction that he was never contacted by the police with regard to this police complaint, that his testimony changed or evolved to finally indicate he had been contacted by the Czech police and that he has not been a credible or trustworthy witness with regard to the alleged skinhead attack in the Czech Republic, which was the central incident described in his PIF narrative and a significant catalyst for him and the associated claimants to leave the Czech Republic.

In the context of the negative determinations above, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the alleged skinhead attack in XXXXX in XXXXXX of 2008 did not take place and has been invented by the principal claimant to support these refugee claims. For all of the negative determinations noted above, the Panel draws an adverse credibility finding with regard to the principal claimant as a credible and trustworthy witness. Discrimination vs. Persecution and the Issue of Nexus

The claimants' counsel in his oral submissions basically indicated that the claimants have a nexus to the Convention refugee definition of race, nationality, and/or membership in a particular social group as it related to their persecution as an ethnic Romani.
The Panel does not agree with these submissions.

The documentary evidence shows that an estimated 80,000 of the country's (the Czech Republic) 200,000 to 250,000 Roma inhabit some 300 so-called "socially excluded localities". Socially excluded localities are residential enclaves mainly populated by Roma that have limited access to formal employment, education, and adequate housing. After considering the documentary evidence presented and counsel's oral submissions, the Panel concludes that some Czech people, including some people in positions of authority, are discriminatory against people of Roma ethnicity. In the case at bar, the principal claimant admitted that he and the female claimant lived among the general Czech population in rented premises, he steadily worked at various positions in the Czech Republic, which is corroborated by his responses to question#7 of his PIF12, and he had little difficulty finding a job, even after being laid off on one occasion. On a similar note, the daughter claimant was able to secure an apartment through her boyfriend's mother and she had been able to attend trade school to XXXXXXXX but she was having difficulty finding employment. In assessing this evidence, the claimants before the Panel appear to be exceptions with regard to marginalization or discrimination since these claimants do not live in any Romani ghettos and that the minor claimants, XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXX, do not attend 'special' Roma schools but they attended mainstream Czech Republic schools. Notwithstanding counsel's latter submissions with regard the Roma ethnicity of these specific claimants, while it is difficult to understand racial attitudes, the Panel determines that the specific behaviour towards these claimants does not reach the level of persecution. Cumulatively for many Romani in the Czech Republic, the effect has been to marginalize Roma people and the Panel notes that the documentary evidence indicates that Roma are generally under-employed, under-educated, frequently live in subsistence housing, and are subject to violence from racially motivated radical groups. These are complex social issues that must be viewed in the context of the state and its reaction to alleviate such discrimination and criminal acts. State Protection

The Panel, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection, and the Panel has applied those principles to the case at bar.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. The Panel is not obliged to prove that the Czech Republic can offer the claimants effective state protection; rather the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that adequate state protection exists. To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence to show the state's inability to protect its citizens.13 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Panel, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.14

The Panel determines that the claimants have been provided with adequate state protection in the Czech Republic. Notwithstanding the principal claimant's opinion with regard to the alleged lack of assistance the principal and female claimant were subjected to in XXXXXX of 2008 (which the Panel has determined is an invented narrative), if the principal claimant's testimony has any ring of truth, the Czech police on this occasion did take a report and these authorities did indicate by correspondence that the investigation has been closed because the police have not been able to identify these "unknown persons". The Panel finds that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. In this particular case as noted above, the principal claimant has provided no corroborating information or documents to suggest that police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the principal and female claimants' allegations that they were attacked by skinheads. Although counsel has suggested in oral submissions that the police document closing this investigation was sent a week after the alleged incident allegedly occurred is indicative that little or nothing was done by the Czech police, the Panel notes that there is no dated police letter before it to confirm a lack of police assistance, even though the letter was allegedly sent and received by the principal claimant (which the Panel has disputed). In view of this evidence and the principles outlined above, the Panel finds that the claimants have not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in the Czech Republic is inadequate.

The Panel notes that the documentary evidence indicates that the ethnic Romani have faced various forms of discrimination in the Czech Republic. The documentary evidence indicates that, although there are few statistics available with regard to police treatment of Roma, Freedom House's Nations in Transit 2008 report for the Czech Republic indicates that violent attacks on foreigners and the Roma minority have declined since the 1990s and remain largely out of the headlines.15 Further, "the judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGO's."16 The documentary evidence17 notes that societal prejudice against the country's Romani population occasionally manifested itself in violence. Members and sympathizers of neo-Nazi organizations were the most frequent perpetrators of acts of interethnic violence, particularly against Roma. The same document indicates that ultranationalists were also active.

The principal, female and daughter claimants have testified that their agents of persecution/harm have been at the hands of skinheads but that their family has also been involved in racist incidents at their respective schools, work places, on buses and at hospitals. The Panel acknowledges that societal prejudice against Roma exists in the Czech society; however, the documentary evidence18 indicates that the state does not condone or acquiesce to this racial and discriminatory behavior, particularly at the hands of extremist skinheads or other fascist groups. Counsel in his oral submissions has suggested that the authorities, the police and the state prosecutor are not attending to or are proceeding improperly with regard to two Roma youths being killed in Tanvald. In reviewing this documentary evidence19 the Panel determines counsel's oral outline of the facts surrounding this incident was actually a distorted opinion of what the Czech authorities are doing. The article indicates that the matter was being investigated properly by the Czech police and the authorities. The Czech police and local Roma Tanvald Association were working together with regard to a public commemoration for the victims, they did add extra security forces and there were plans to bring in more security / police, if required. As well, the state prosecutor was giving timely information regard to how the authorities were proceeding with regard to the investigation of this incident. In other words, the latter article is not proof that the authorities are turning a blind eye or not assisting the Romani in the Czech republic. Similarly, the within the same exhibit, the Panel has reviewed another article20 with regard to a Romani woman murdered by three youths in Prague. The Panel determines that the Czech police are investigating this incident, however, in the opinion of the Panel, this appears to be an attack on homeless people or "...basically anyone they felt like targeting", as opposed to a racially motivated attack against Romas. In this latter article, based on the evidence, the authorities have charged one of the youth with murder, therefore, the Panel determines that the Czech authorities are responding properly to attacks against other minorites, which includes the homeless in that country.

On a more positive note with regard to the Czech government's Anti-Extremism Strategy, in the mid-1990s, the Ministry of the Interior launched an initiative to combat extremism, allowing for police monitoring of extremist group activities and trends. The initiative began with the creation of a specialized anti-extremist department within the Police Presidium of the Czech Republic in 1995, followed by the deployment of anti-extremist specialists at the regional and district level in 1996. The Panel notes there are between 130 and 140 extremist crime investigators across the country, with two members assigned to each region and one to each district. The tasks of the various anti-extremism offices, which rely on information, gathered from sources such as criminologists, crime prevention department personnel and the local police include: preventing and combating extremism and racially motivated crime against all minorities; working with minority communities through NGOs; raising awareness in schools; and communicating with local authorities about extremism. According to the Ministry of the Interior, anti-extremist measures have shown increasing signs of success. Claimants' counsel's own documentary evidence21 indicates that the Czech police are making significant efforts to deal with neo-Nazis demonstrating in the country. In other words, the Czech authorities are not simply sitting on their hands and allowing racism to run rampant or unchecked in the Czech Republic.

The Panel also determines that, although the Czech government faces challenges in combating discrimination and racism, the RPD documentary evidence22 does include examples showing that the authorities, including the police, respond adequately to violence by racist Czechs and extremist groups through legislative measures and police action on the ground.

With regard to police protection measures established by the state to address acts of discrimination and racially motivated violence, the Panel notes that governmental interlocutors pointed to Roma Police Assistants (RPAs), Minority Liaison Officers (MLOs), and the Ministry of the Interior's Anti-Extremism Strategy. In addition, the Ministry of the Interior's Strategy on Policing Minorities (2008-2012) was passed on 9 April 2008 under Government Resolution No. 384. The main objectives of this strategy include training on policing minority communities, efforts to employ minorities into the police force, researching crime in socially excluded localities, as well as maintaining the MLO and RPA initiatives.

Holomek of the SRNM believed that RPAs would be more effective if they were employed as police officers. The police in Brno asserted that having RPAs work in NGOs is better for building trust with Romani communities. RPA duties include establishing contact between Roma and the police, accompanying Romani victims of crime who wish to file a police report, educating victims on their legal rights and responsibilities, helping police investigate unreported crime and assisting in the provision of social services in socially excluded localities.

Several NGO interlocutors also identified the existence of the RPA program as a sign of progress and two interlocutors claimed that RPAs have increased Romani trust in the police. For instance, representatives of DROM, a Brno-based NGO that provides social and legal assistance to Roma, reported that they have seen a general increase in Roma seeking assistance from RPAs. Additionally, MLOs are employed by the Ministry of the Interior (unlike RPAs) to help introduce police to minority groups and to communicate with NGOs and local authorities with a focus on crime prevention. MLOs also participate in projects intended to combat the social exclusion of Roma. For example, Ministry of the Interior interlocutors stated that MLOs are involved in the project "Joint World" which is aimed at attending to alcohol and drug abuse in socially excluded localities. Two NGO interlocutors commended the effectiveness of MLOs, and the Ministry of the Interior stated that MLO activities had improved communication between police and Roma, contributing to a reduction of crime within Romani communities.

The Panel determines that the examples contained in documentary evidence outlined above indicates that the Czech government has put in place infrastructure whereby the claimants would have recourse available to seek protection if they were to be discriminated against and thus face alleged persecution, or if they were to be denied security services due to their Roma ethnicity upon return to the Czech Republic. The documentary evidence23 indicates that there is legal redress available if Roma are denied or provided inadequate security services due to their ethnicity. Citizens can register "complaints about police inaction and non-serious offenses by police officers" with the Office of Internal Control, which is part of the Police of the Czech Republic. Citizens do so by sending an email or by contacting by telephone. The complaints will either be immediately addressed or "submitted for inspection" to the responsible bodies.

The Panel notes with regard to the reports from the Embassy of the Czech Republic, in addition to the police complaints investigation bodies, the Czech Republic has a Public Defender of Rights - Ombudsman. The Public Defender of Rights is responsible for protecting citizens against the improper conduct of authorities and other institutions when this conduct is: i) against the law; ii) strays outside the democratic principles and principles of good administration, or iii) in case the authorities remain inactive towards specific cases. As part of the government's overall efforts to improve the position of the Roma, the Public Defender "set up a separate Equal Treatment Department, where six staff handle specific cases of the application of discriminatory practices to Czech citizens". Services offered by this department include "methodological assistance to discrimination victims," "legal assessments of cases of discrimination," and "advise [sic] or ... cooperation in obtaining evidence". Approximately 20 percent of cases handled by this department involve discrimination against Roma. If a complaint does not fall under the mandate of the Public Defender, the complainant is provided with contact information for NGOs that might be able to help, which the Panel finds would be of assistance to the principal, female and daughter claimants given their alleged dissatisfaction with the Czech police. Moreover, if the complaint is submitted to a unit that is not responsible, the unit will pass the complaint to the responsible unit and inform the complainant. The documentary evidence24 shows that the various departments outline protocol and provide step-by-step guidance to citizens, which would be of assistance to the principal claimant and his family, to ensure that any complaints are properly filed and registered and, thereafter, followed through by the authorities.

Having canvassed the country condition documents, the Panel determines that the Czech Republic is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. Notwithstanding counsel's submissions that the claimants would not be able to access state protection in the Czech Republic should they return to their home country, the Panel finds the documentary evidence indicates that the claimants, considering their particular circumstances, would have recourses available upon their return to the Czech Republic to obtain state protection, and to seek redress if the police were to refuse to respond or if the principal, female and daughter claimants were to believe that their complaints were not being taken seriously. There are numerous examples in the documentary evidence to demonstrate the Czech Republic's willingness and ability to protect its Romani citizens.25 The Panel understands and sympathizes with the claimants' frustration with regard to racial incidents in the Czech Republic; however, no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.26 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.27 Further, while police agencies of the state have an obligation to protect, none can ensure the result.28

The daughter claimants' children have allegedly had problems at school. The Panel acknowledges that societal prejudice against Roma exists in the Czech society; however, the government is actively engaged in the integration of the Roma communities in the Czech society.29 With regard to education, compared to previous years, there is a continuing increase in the number of supported projects in the key areas of pre-school preparation of Romani children and the education of pupils from the Roma community at primary school. This trend can be seen as positive.30

In secondary education there is a targeted programme of "Support for Roma Secondary School Students", which can be viewed positively for the minor claimants. As part of this programme, the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport supported a total of 2,715 applications in 2007 in the amount of CZK 9,939,300. The aim of the aforementioned programme is to support the studies of Romani students whose parents would find the costs of secondary education a considerable financial burden. Support for Roma university students is addressed through public university Development Programmes, respectively, programmes for the support of handicapped students and applicants from disadvantaged social groups. A highly motivational programme is the Roma Memorial University Scholarship awarded by the Roma Educational Fund. In the past, this programme was administered by the Open Society Institute in Budapest.31

Documentary evidence32 shows that there is a visible trend that shows an improvement in the overall education level of Roma. Romani children and adolescents achieve a higher level of education than their parents or grandparents. This improvement is particularly evident in the growing number of pupils and students at secondary schools and universities. There are systematic programmes of targeted assistance such as preparatory classes, teacher's assistants and projects supporting the integration of Roma into mainstream education; nevertheless, these are limited by the definition of the target group (socially disadvantaged children, pupils and students) used by the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport in targeting programmes directed at Roma. This definition is based on Act No. 561/2004 Coll., on pre-school, primary, secondary, technical and other education (the Education Act); however, Romani children often face not only social exclusion but also national differences and must often deal with the prejudices and stereotypes of majority society. In this respect, the Ministry have started the process of systemic and curricular changes. For these reasons, the Panel determines that the Czech government is continuing to address issues relating to discriminatory practices in education and has brought about change in the delivery of education for Romani children and adults. The Panel, however, does acknowledge that the disparities in education levels continue to exist.

In the area of housing, the general objective is the endeavour to prevent the establishment of new segregated localities to improve the situation in the already existing segregated Roma localities and to improve access to housing by socially weaker Roma. With regard to health, it is noted that socially excluded Roma communities are currently facing a problem of a low level of awareness about the possibilities of health prevention and care. The Czech Ministry of Health has taken steps to target priority areas to improve delivery of health care.

The principal claimant has testified that their main problem is racism from skinheads and racist people in the Czech Republic. Based on the documentary evidence,33 the Panel acknowledges that Roma in the Czech Republic are discriminated against and are victims of violence from extremist groups; however, the Panel finds that the Czech government is actively engaged in addressing racism and racist practices against Roma through legislation, programmes and initiatives, coordination with non-governmental agencies, and more importantly through allocation of resources to enable communities to implement legislative and other measures.

The Panel specifically notes that the Czech Republic is not an island unto its own, but it is a responsible member of the European Union and reports regularly to the governance structures within that Union. Even if criticism of the Czech Republic's measures to combat racism is warranted, particularly against the Romani population, on a balance of probabilities, as the Panel has outlined above, the Czech Republic is taking the measures to implement the standards that are mandated as a member of the European Union.

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced, including the claimants' testimonies and counsel's oral submissions, the Panel determines that the claimants, in their particular situation and circumstances, have not satisfied the burden by providing clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming if the claimants should need it upon their return to the Czech Republic. Section 97(1) (b) (iv) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

If the Panel understands counsel's submissions, counsel has basically submitted that the claimants are in need of protection because section 97(1)(b)(iv) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act is not applicable and the health care system in the Czech Republic persecutes them, due to the fact that the Roma live 14 years less than other Czech nationals. Counsel cited the decision of Covarrubias, Katia Montano v. M.C.I.34, within which the President of the Court of Appeal, on that occasion, indicated that section 97(1)(b)(iv) is not applicable if the health care is denied to an individual on persecutorial grounds. The Panel does not find that this submission is applicable in the case at bar. The Panel notes, if the principal claimant's testimony with regard to the XXXXXX of 2008 attack against him and his wife has any ring of truth (which the Panel has disputed), he testified that after this incident he was satisfied with the care he received from the personnel at the medical clinic in XXXXX. In sharp contrast to the latter statement, both the female and daughter claimants were not satisfied with the medical treatment that had received in their country.

During his oral submissions, counsel has referred to the claimants' documentary evidence, which outlines various incidents of poor treatment or denial of medical treatment for ethnic Romani. In fact, he submits that the Romani are persecuted when it comes to health care.
The Panel does not agree.

With regard to health, the Panel notes that socially excluded Roma communities are currently facing a problem of a low level of awareness about the possibilities of health prevention and care. The Czech Ministry of Health has taken steps to target priority areas to improve delivery of health care.

Within the claimant's own documentary evidence is the report35 of "Health Needs of the Roma Population in the Czech and Slovak Republic, which was commissioned by the World Bank and the European Centre on Health of Societies in Transition written by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, U.K. in collaboration with the Department of Social Medicine and Health Care Administration Masaryk University, Brno, Czech Republic. Within the report, there are findings that indicate there is a lower life expectancy for Romas, which counsel has alleged is a result of poor medical health for the Romani in the Czech Republic; however, the Panel notes this same report indicates this fact is actually due to a number of significant factors, which include poor hygiene which leads to diseases such as hepatitis A, parasites, bacteria and viruses and TB36. The report also stated that one out of every three children under a year old that is hospitalized is Roma, although Roma represent less than 3% of the population.37 Moreover, there is a 21.5% prevalence of mental retardation of Roma compared to 0.9% of non Roma; however, the report indicates this is attributable in part due to the problem of inbreeding and also the high prevalence of certain genetic diseases.38 The Panel notes that the same report also mentions the unhealthy lifestyle of the Roma including a high prevalence of smoking, low consumption of fruit and vegetables, obesity and consumption of alcohol.39 Furthermore, the report indicated that there was non-compliance with prescribed treatment by the Roma.40

In the context of the documentary evidence noted above, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the shorter lifespan of the Roma as argued by counsel cannot be attributed to denial of health care to the Roma on persecutorial grounds. It is clear from the report that there are several factors as previously mentioned including lifestyle and dietary habits that contribute to their shorter lifespan. It is noteworthy that report indicates that 77% of Roma considered the medical care that they and their families received to be adequate.41 For these reasons, the Panel rejects the argument that the claimants would be denied medical care because they are ethnic Romani.

For all of the cumulative negative determinations outlined above, the Panel determines that that the principal claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA. This negative determination extends to the female, daughter and minor claimants, who must rely on the principal claimant's testimony to support their respective claims.

The Refugee Protection Division rejects all of these respective claims. (signed) "Paul Robinson" Paul G.C.
